blocks.heading: Relations
blocks.text: A relation from A to B is a subset of the Cartesian product A × B. It is a set of ordered pairs (x, y), where x is in A and y is in B. Example: {(−2, 1), (4, 3), (7, −3)}.

blocks.heading: Domain and range
blocks.text: The domain is the set of first components of a relation. The range is the set of second components actually used. The codomain is the specified set of possible outputs. The range is a subset of it and need not use every possible output.

blocks.heading: Relation as a table
blocks.text:
<mspace=0.72em>x     y
−2    1
−2    3
 0   −3
 1    4
 3    1</mspace>

Each row is an ordered pair. The repeated input −2 has two outputs, so this relation is not a function.

blocks.heading: The same relation as a graph
blocks.text: Plot each ordered pair as a point (x, y).

blocks.heading: The same relation as a mapping
blocks.text: An arrow from x to y represents the pair (x, y).

blocks.heading: Special relations
blocks.text: On a set A, the empty relation contains no ordered pairs. The universal relation is A × A. The identity relation contains exactly the pairs (a, a) for a in A. The inverse relation reverses every pair: (a, b) becomes (b, a).

blocks.heading: Properties of relations
blocks.text: A relation on A is reflexive if every (a, a) is included. It is symmetric if (a, b) implies (b, a). It is transitive if (a, b) and (b, c) imply (a, c). A reflexive relation may contain pairs beyond the identity relation.

blocks.heading: Functions
blocks.text: A function from A to B assigns each element of A exactly one output in B. One input cannot have two different outputs. Different inputs may share an output. {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 5)} is a function.

blocks.heading: Function examples
blocks.text:
The identity relation {(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (4, 4)} is a function.

{(−2, 4), (−1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4)} is also a function: each input has one output.

{(1, 0), (0, 1), (−1, 0), (0, −1)} is not: input 0 has two different outputs.

blocks.heading: Injective and many-to-one
blocks.text: An injective, or one-to-one, function sends distinct inputs to distinct outputs. A many-to-one function sends at least two different inputs to the same output. This is allowed for a function.

blocks.heading: Surjective and bijective
blocks.text: A surjective, or onto, function uses every element of its specified codomain as an output. A bijective function is both injective and surjective. Each codomain element has exactly one preimage.

blocks.heading: One-to-one mapping
blocks.text: Each input has one output, and no two inputs share an output.

blocks.heading: Many-to-one mapping
blocks.text: Several inputs share output 0 or 1. Each input still has exactly one output.

blocks.heading: A relation that is not a function
blocks.text: Inputs 7 and 2 each have two outputs. A function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input.

blocks.heading: Vertical line test
blocks.text: For a graph in the Cartesian plane to represent y as a function of x, every vertical line must meet it at at most one point. A vertical line with two intersections identifies one input with two outputs.

blocks.heading: A graph that passes the test
blocks.text: Every vertical line meets this curve at most once.

blocks.heading: A graph that fails the test
blocks.text: Two intersections give one input two outputs. This relation is not a function.
